summary.text: Volcanoes are vents that let lava, ash and gases escape from magma below, and geologists group them by time, place, structure and composition.
Those at diverging plates, such as mid-ocean ridges, are usually nonexplosive, while those at converging plates, such as the Pacific Ring of Fire, erupt violently.
By eruption history they are called active, dormant or extinct, and some erupt just once while others have many periods of activity.

items.prompt: Two plates slide sideways past each other along a long boundary. What volcanic activity would you expect there?

options.label: Gentle lava flows all along it

items.explain: Volcanoes are usually not created at transform boundaries, where plates slide past one another.

items.prompt: Where are most of Earth's volcanoes found?
items.explain: Most plate boundaries are underwater, so most volcanoes, and most volcanic activity, are underwater too.

items.prompt: At a subduction zone, an ocean plate sinks and releases water into the hot rock above it. What does that water do?

options.label: Cools the rock so nothing melts
Raises the pressure to keep rock solid
Lowers its melting point, making magma

items.explain: In flux melting, water from the sinking plate lowers the melting temperature of the mantle wedge above, creating magma.

items.prompt: A volcano has erupted several times but not in the last 20,000 years, and it still has a magma source. How is it classed?
items.explain: Dormant volcanoes have not erupted since about 12,000 years ago but may erupt again; extinct ones have no magma source.

items.prompt: A tectonic plate drifts steadily over a fixed plume of hot rock rising from deep below. What builds up at the surface over time?

options.label: A line of volcanoes, newest one active
A ring of volcanoes around the plume

items.explain: As the plate moves, each volcano goes inactive as it drifts off the plume and a new one forms over it, as in Hawaii.

items.prompt: Hot mantle rock rises slowly beneath a mid-ocean ridge without being heated further. Why does it begin to melt?

options.label: Friction between the plates heats it
Seawater seeps down and melts it
The pressure on it drops as it rises
The core sends it a burst of heat

items.explain: The falling pressure in rising mantle rock leads to partial melting, making magma and new ocean crust.
